title: How cycling legends were born: Nicole Cooke claims gold for Britain

How cycling legends were born: Nicole Cooke claims gold for Britain

In early December 2007 Nicole Cooke was in China. Despite not being in a positive frame of mind, she had travelled to Beijing to research the 2008 Olympic Games Road Race circuit. A few months earlier Cooke had closed her season, losing her World Cup lead in the final round of the series before going straight into surgery in a bid to resolve a long-standing knee injury that had impacted the second half of the year. A period of rehab had followed but by November the knee pain had returned.

‘I was distraught,’ Cooke writes in her autobiography The Breakaway. ‘I couldn’t take it anymore; I wanted to stop and end my career there and then.’

Nevertheless Cooke had already booked flight tickets to Beijing. So she went, ignoring thoughts that maybe her career was effectively over, and inspected the course. Cooke rode the circuit’s main climb and bore the pain of sprinting on the uphill drag to the finish line, banking the details. Then she went home to try to get fit.

The start of 2008 proved as difficult for Cooke as the end of 2007 had been. Her season began late due to needing to recover from that knee injury – her first race coming at the end of March – and then came issues with her team.

Cooke had signed for a Halfords-sponsored outfit of British riders, run by British Cycling, in the belief their season would be structured around her Olympic ambitions. But her plans were hit when the team announced that they would not be riding in June’s Grande Boucle Féminine Internationale. It was a race that Cooke viewed as vital to her Olympic preparations and one where she was the two-time defending champion.

The team’s decision forced Cooke to look elsewhere, and she was able to secure a last-minute ride with the Swift team. Despite the disruption, she recorded a string of top five stage finishes at the Grand Boucle, including a strong ride in the Alps to claim second on the stage to Sestriere on her way to finishing third overall. A week later Cooke took her ninth British Road Race title. She was back on track. Now for the Olympics.

Fighting for Olympic Gold

Sixty-six riders started the women’s Olympic Road Race. Ahead lay a 126km route, including a run-in of 78km to two laps of a hilly 23km circuit that featured the final haul to the finish line Cooke had ridden eight months previously.

The British team comprised Cooke, Emma Pooley and Sharon Laws. Cooke writes that the final pre-race meeting was ‘far removed from a proper professional team meeting prior to a critical race’, with instructions being simply for Laws to cover moves in the approach to the circuit, Pooley to attack on the climb and ‘Nicole, be ready for the finish’.

The weather for the previous day’s men’s race had been hot and dry but the gloomy conditions that initially greeted the women soon turned to heavy rain. It made for treacherous conditions with riders losing control, crashing and landing heavily in the deep gutters that lined the roads.

As the bell sounded for the final lap, Russia’s Natalia Boyarskaya was leading the race. Pooley then launched her effort, soon joined by Italy’s Tatiana Guderzo. They caught Boyarskaya to form a trio of riders leading the race. Behind, Cooke sat tight until Germany’s Judith Arndt responded, then she followed her move.

With the three leaders caught, a flurry of moves and counter-moves went and came back, steadily reducing the main group of favourites in the process. As the finale neared, five riders remained in contention: Emma Johansson, Christine Soeder, Linda Villumsen, Guderzo and Cooke.

Reading through Cooke’s recollection of the final moments of this race reveals the extent of split-second tactical decisions that a rider undertakes in these highly dynamic situations. Where are the dangers? Who is riding on whose wheel? What does that tell me about how they are feeling? How should I use that information? How do they view what I am doing? If I hang back here, how will the others react? Will they attack or call my bluff? What is the next pinch point? Can I exploit that or is it too risky? All thoughts and decisions made instinctively and quickly through years of experience, all while on the point of exhaustion.

Cooke, worried about the possibility of getting caught in a crash in the wet conditions, chose to sit at the back of the leading group as the last technical bends were negotiated. She risked losing touch and had to launch her final effort earlier as a result.

‘It was going to be a very long sprint for me,’ Cooke writes. ‘I was catching them quickly and took the risk of taking the lead and the inside line around the last bend.’

With 200m to go, she hit the front.

‘My legs were already burning from the effort I had made to get into this position, but I wasn’t going to let the pain stop me. This was the moment I’d been dreaming of since I was 12, fighting for the Olympic gold medal.’

That final uphill sprint seemed to take an eternity as Cooke gritted her teeth. In the face of huge efforts from Johansson and Guderzo, Cooke clung on and crossed the line to claim gold, screaming in celebration. She had just become the first, and to date only, Briton to win the Olympic Road Race.

‘I just came over the line and there was so much in me,’ Cooke said afterwards. ‘So many emotions that all came out at once. I was not composed enough to take my hands off the bars, so much of it came out as noise because that’s just the person I am.’

On her return to Wales, Cooke’s home village of Wick, in the Vale of Glamorgan, threw a celebratory party featuring an open-topped bus tour, speeches, children’s bike races and the unveiling of a commemorative plaque.

‘It was the most perfect occasion,’ Cooke later reflected.

A little under seven weeks later, she was on the start line of the World Championships Road Race in Varese, Italy. She had been on three Worlds podiums before but had never stood on the top step. This time it would be different. After refusing to lead the pursuit of numerous attacks in the closing kilometres, Cooke briefly made her own effort, then sat up and watched Johansson make a move with the final kilometre approaching.

She resisted any temptation to follow, waiting for others to lead the chase. Into the final moments Johansson still led but the gap was now coming down fast. First Judith Arndt, then Cooke, then Marianne Vos blew past the Swedish rider. This was the podium, but in what order?

Arndt tired in the final 150m, leaving a two-up drag race to the line with Cooke taking the win ahead of Vos.

‘I was quite happy to see the race play out because so close to the finish I knew I wasn’t going to win if I chased Emma [Johansson],’ Cooke reflected. ‘[I thought] chasing her won’t help so I’m not going to… it was quite logical.’

With that win Cooke became the first rider in history to win both the Olympics Road Race and the rainbow jersey in the same year.

‘It was a dream come true in Beijing,’ Cooke said after her Worlds win, ‘and today as well. I don’t think I’ve realised it yet. I need some time to let it sink in.’
